catalog_quote: El acento en la palabra ashéninca no es fonémico y puede predecirse con cierta facilidad en función de dos tipos de principios que se traslapan. El primero se basa en la posición de la sílaba en relación con el principio de la palabra; el segundo, y el más fuerte, tiene que ver con la "fuerza" de la sílaba misma basada en sus propiedades fonéticas. [...] La sílaba fuerte (C)VV(N) siempre está acentuada, mientras que las sílabas débiles /si/ o /ȼhi/ casi nunca llevan acento. La sílaba normal CV solamente lleva acento cuando la configuración de la palabra así lo determina. [...] Si una palabra no posee sílabas fuertes, el acento recae en las sílabas alternas, empezando de la segunda sílaba de la palabra. Nótese, sin embargo, que la sílaba CV en posición final de palabra nunca lleva acento [...] La palabra ashéninca, en muchos casos, lleva varios acentos; pero el acento primario se asigna …
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: ajyi1238 is not in the catalog. Of the three search titles: Spring 1990 (Arizona diss.) is about this language's stress only as a theoretical treatment of Payne's data (stress pp. 58-68 per McCarthy & Prince) and could not be obtained (repository.arizona.edu 403; no HathiTrust record; J. Payne 1990 'Asheninca stress patterns' is about the Pichis dialect (SIL's own entry tags it cpu; McGarrity 2003:177), already carried in the catalog under pich1237, host volume restricted on archive.org/HathiTrust - low priority for this language; Black 1991 (PASC 2) is a foot-typology/reduplication/velar-glide paper, print-only per the UCSC publications page, its Phonology sibling paywalled - low priority. The real gain of this search of works with stress in the title is the primary: via the MPG PuRe records' external links to SIL archive entries 8521/29935 and the the Internet Archive (the SIL file store is behind an automated-access block), I downloaded Payne, Payne & Sánchez Santos 1982 (SLP 18, 311 pp.) and scanned its stress chapter (pp. 185-195, verified against page images): first-hand Apurucayali rules - every (C)VV(N) stressed, CVN stressed unless next to (C)VV(N), alternating stress from the second light syllable, word-final CV never stressed, disyllables initial, si/chi extra-light, primary = last strong syllable within the last four syllables else the last rhythmic stress, optional secondaries, a handful of final-stressed vocatives/emphatics. Payne 1981 (also downloaded via the Internet Archive) is explicitly silent on stress placement and defers to the 1982 volume. The 1980 ILV dictionary's orthographic stress rules (first reading) agree with the 1982 statement.

new_statements.quote: 2. Una sílaba con vocal doblada o con diptongo (es decir una sílaba fuerte) se acentúa cuando no está en posición final de palabra. […] 4. En una serie de tres o más sílabas que constan de una sola vocal (es decir, sílabas regulares), se acentúa la segunda de cada par de sílabas, a partir de la segunda sílaba regular de la serie, pero nunca se acentúa una sílaba regular que es final de palabra o que va inmediatamente seguida por una sílaba fuerte. […] 6. […] se asigna la acentuación principal a la última sílaba fuerte de una palabra si ocupa el lugar penúltimo, antepenúltimo o anterior al antepenúltimo. Si no, se asigna la acentuación principal a la última sílaba acentuada de la palabra.
new_statements.translation: 2. A syllable with a doubled vowel or a diphthong (that is, a strong syllable) is stressed when it is not in word-final position. […] 4. In a series of three or more syllables consisting of a single vowel (that is, regular syllables), the second of each pair of syllables is stressed, starting from the second regular syllable of the series, but a regular syllable that is word-final or that is immediately followed by a strong syllable is never stressed. […] 6. […] the principal stress is assigned to the last strong syllable of a word if it occupies the penultimate, antepenultimate or pre-antepenultimate position. If not, the principal stress is assigned to the last stressed syllable of the word.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable from syllable weight and position (the dictionary writes no tildes because 'las reglas siempre predicen el lugar de la mayor fuerza de voz', p. 11). Heavy syllables (long vowel or diphthong) are stressed unless word-final; in a run of light syllables, feet are built left to right and the second syllable of each pair is stressed (iambic), but never a word-final light syllable nor a light syllable immediately preceding a heavy one; disyllabic words stress the first syllable. Among the stressed syllables, primary stress goes to the last heavy syllable provided it is the penult, antepenult or pre-antepenult; otherwise to the rightmost stressed syllable (i.e., the penult in odd-parity light words like irírori, coviyaníri; the antepenult in even-parity words like iràpanántsi). McCarthy & Prince 1993 (Appendix A.2, from Payne, Payne & Sánchez Santos 1982:185-195, Apurucayali specifically) confirm the same system: left-to-right iambs (LL)/(LH)/(H), final syllables unstressed unless diphthongal, hence trochaic disyllables (círi, máto), CVN counting as heavy.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Rule 6 marks the non-principal stressed syllables with a grave accent as 'acentuación secundaria' (sàasáatzi, máaquirìtzi, cocànirόqui, otàntotáantsi). Rule 7 (p. 13): optionally a secondary stress with high tone is assigned to a penultimate light syllable lacking the vowel i when it follows a stressed light syllable with i (iquithóqui ~ iquìthóqui 'moneda'). Rule 8 (p. 13): when an initial heavy syllable is followed by two light syllables the first of which lacks i, the secondary stress optionally moves to the syllable right after the heavy one (máicavàtzi ~ máicàvatzi). McCarthy & Prince 1993 add, from PP&S 1982:193, that penult secondary stress in long even-parity words 'is variably realized under complex conditions'.
new_statements.exceptions: Rule 1: some words, mostly vocatives and words with the superlative distal demonstrative -ntóo and the exclamative -vée, have final stress (charinée 'abuelo', jantóo 'allá lejos', quitàiterivée 'buenos días'); these are the only words written with a tilde. Rule 3: disyllables stress the first syllable except when it is shi or tsi with unpronounced i, in which case the final syllable is stressed (tsicá '¿qué?' vs sári, mápi, tzíri). Rule 5: when a syllable due for stress by rule 4 is shi/tsi with silent i, the stress falls on the immediately preceding syllable (ótsitzi 'perro', páshine 'otro', cátsicona, pitzìríshipa). Heavy syllables in word-final position are not stressed (rule 2), though McCarthy & Prince 1993 show final diphthongs stressed in PP&S 1982 data (kitìšitàkotái, àatái).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, dictionary citation forms (nouns unpossessed with -ntsi/-tsi, verbs with infinitive -aantsi/-taantsi); vocatives excepted. The rules are stated for 'el idioma asheninca' without regional qualification, the dictionary covering the Pichis (PI), Apurucayali (AP) and Alto Ucayali/Alto Yuruá (UC) regions (p. 4; Alto Perené and Gran Pajonal excluded).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source is David Payne's 1980 multidialectal Ashéninca dictionary, whose stress rules are stated for 'el idioma asheninca' as a whole; the preliminary edition covers the Pichis (PI = Glottolog pich1237, ISO cpu), Apurucayali (AP = ajyi1238, ISO cpc) and Alto Ucayali/Alto Yuruá (UC = Ucayali-Yurúa Ashéninka, ISO cpb, Glottolog ucay1237 if I have the code right) regions and excludes Alto Perené and Gran Pajonal (p. 4). Payne is the author of the Apurucayali monograph (Payne 1981) and his co-compiler Jorge Sánchez Santos co-authored its 1982 Spanish revision; McCarthy & Prince 1993's rendering of the Apurucayali-specific data (PP&S 1982:185-195) shows the same system (LR iambs, heavy always stressed except finally, final light syllables never stressed, extra-weak s/ch syllables), so the statement is taken as applying to ajyi1238, with the Apurucayali-specific books listed first in the list of works to obtain.

new_statements.quote: La sílaba fuerte (C)VV(N) siempre está acentuada, mientras que las sílabas débiles /si/ o /čhi/ casi nunca llevan acento. [...] Si una palabra no posee sílabas fuertes, el acento recae en las sílabas alternas, empezando de la segunda sílaba de la palabra. [...] la sílaba CV en posición final de palabra nunca lleva acento [...] La última sílaba fuerte (C)VV(N) o CVN lleva acento primario si se encuentra dentro de las cuatro últimas sílabas de la palabra; de no ser así, el último acento asignado es el primario.
new_statements.translation: The strong syllable (C)VV(N) is always stressed, whereas the weak syllables /si/ or /chi/ almost never carry stress. [...] If a word has no strong syllables, stress falls on alternate syllables, starting from the second syllable of the word. [...] a CV syllable in word-final position never carries stress [...] The last strong syllable (C)VV(N) or CVN carries primary stress if it lies within the last four syllables of the word; if not, the last stress assigned is the primary one.

Serie Lingüística Peruana 18. Lima/Yarinacocha: Ministerio de Educación & Instituto Lingüístico de Verano. Capítulo X 'El acento' (Judith Payne principal author).

new_statements.reading: Predictable, non-phonemic, quantity-sensitive stress. Rhythm: every (C)VV(N) syllable (long vowel/diphthong) is stressed (except phrase-finally, where stress retracts to the preceding syllable); CVN is stressed unless adjacent to a (C)VV(N); over runs of light CV syllables, stress falls left-to-right on every second syllable counting from the word beginning or from the last stressed/strong syllable, i.e. iambic, with the word-final CV never stressed and the CV immediately before a strong syllable unstressed; disyllables stress the initial syllable; extra-light si/chi push stress to the preceding syllable (or to the final in disyllables before a voiceless consonant). Culminative primary stress: the last strong syllable if it is within the last four syllables (in practice penult, antepenult or preantepenult, since the final is never stressed), otherwise the last stress assigned by the rhythm rule. Optional secondary stresses on non-high vowels; a small set of vocative/emphatic words with final stress. For a catalog: weight-sensitive (CVV(N) heavy; CVN semi-heavy), iambic left-to-right rhythm with final non-finality, right-edge bounded primary (within a four-syllable window) preferring the last heavy - the same system that Hayes 1995 / McGarrity 2003 / Rasin 2017 render for Pichis after J. Payne 1990, here stated first-hand for Apurucayali.

new_statements.quote: Payne and Payne demonstrate that stress placement is a low level phonetic phenomenon in Axininca based on a strength scale of syllables, without any reference to grammatical brackets or a cycle. Accordingly, CVN and CVV syllables are generally strong and have some degree of stress, while CV syllables are generally weak and correspondingly unstressed. The normal stress pattern for words with only CV syllables is for every alternate syllable to be stressed beginning with the second syllable. [...] the stress phenomena are predictable based on surface syllable and word shape and a scale of syllable strength versus weakness.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog's weight-sensitive record and as the first-hand Payne, Payne & Sánchez 1982 statement (CVV(N) strong and stressed, CV weak, alternating stress from the second syllable in runs of light syllables); explicitly states the non-contrastive/phonetic status ('if it were contrastive', p. 168; 'predictable', p. 169). It is a summary of Payne & Payne (to appear), not a first-hand stress description, and adds nothing on primary stress, the final-syllable exclusion, the si/chi extra-light syllables or the vocative exceptions that the 1982 work gives.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable and non-contrastive (a phonetic, not phonological, rule; not written in the orthography). Heavy syllables CVN and CVV are strong and carry stress; light CV syllables are weak and unstressed; in words consisting only of CV syllables every second syllable is stressed counting from the second syllable (iambic left-to-right alternation), and heavy syllables override that alternation by attracting stress ('The strong syllables perturb this pattern by taking stress when not in these patterns', p. 104). No primary-stress (culminativity) rule and no word-edge domain is given; the book has no stress chapter and defers the formulation to Payne & Payne (to appear) = the 1982 SLP 18 chapter X.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not treated as such; the description is of multiple ('some degree of') stress on every strong syllable plus the alternating pattern, with no primary/secondary distinction stated. pp. 168-169 add that stress and pitch are phonetic rules, 'Nor is stress introduced by a cycle or rules with grammatical environments.'
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. p. 104 speculates that the genitive /N/-insertion rule may have originated as a device to make a syllable strong and hence stressed. p. 159 fn. 14: 'The actual formulations of these and other phonetic rules, as well as stress placement in Axininca, are elaborated in Payne and Payne (to appear).' p. 7 (PDF 20) mentions Pike & Kindberg 1956 'analysis of multiple stress' for Ashaninca (a different variety), not for Axininca.
new_statements.identity_note: Payne 1981 describes 'the dialect spoken on the Apurucayali River and its tributaries, henceforth referred to by the name "Axininca"' (p. 1), data from Puerto Davis (Jorge Sánchez), i.e. exactly ajyi1238. Its remark on the -ni/-ti alternation being suppletive 'in the Ashaninca dialect' and its citation of Pike & Kindberg 1956 'multiple stress' concern Ashaninca, a different variety. Spring 1990 (per its abstract) is on Axininca Campa, same variety.

new_statements.relation_note: Same system as the existing statements from Payne 1980 (Diccionario, 'Normas de acentuación') and Payne, Payne & Sánchez 1982 ch. X: CVV(N) always stressed, CVN heavy but weaker than CVV, iambic alternation from the second syllable over light runs, final syllable never stressed, disyllables initial, culminative main stress on the last heavy within the last four syllables. Spring adds a formal metrical analysis (final-syllable extrametricality, L-to-R iambs on the rhyme projection, no degenerate feet, three-way weight hierarchy CVV > CVN > CV for clash resolution with the nasal coda as a non-moraic rhyme dependent) and states the four-syllable main-stress window explicitly; her data are seco…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Quantity-sensitive iambic rhythm: final syllable extrametrical (never stressed); iambic feet built left to right so that in all-light words stress falls on even-numbered syllables; heavy rhymes (CVV long vowel/diphthong, and CVN with nasal coda) are always stressed even in odd positions; no degenerate feet (penult unstressed when antepenult is stressed); clash resolution on a three-way weight scale CVV > CVN > CV (a mono-moraic rhyme adjacent to a branching/bimoraic rhyme is destressed, so CVN loses to CVV and CV loses to CVN); disyllables stress the initial syllable. Main (primary) stress: a single main stress on the rightmost, heaviest stressed syllable within the final four syllables of the word (not formalized; referred to Spring 1989c). Data explicitly from Payne, Payne & Sanchez 1982 (fn. 17).
new_statements.secondary_stress: The alternating (rhythmic) stresses are the non-main stresses; main stress is culminative on the rightmost heaviest stressed syllable in a four-syllable right-edge window (fn. 25, p. 74). No separate statement on optional secondary stresses beyond the iambic alternation.
new_statements.exceptions: fn. 18 p. 66: 'A couple of morphemes appearing in final position always attract stress. See Payne et al 1982.' fn. 19: the iambic pattern can be altered at the surface by other phonological rules (not discussed; refers to Payne et al 1982, Spring 1989c, Payne 1987 on Pichis). fn. 20 p. 67: three word-initial VN syllables are given as unstressed in Payne et al 1982, but D. Payne (p.c.) believes they are stressed. Disyllables stress the initial vowel (p. 65). fn. 23 p. 70: two adjacent CVN syllables predicted to destress one, no examples found.
new_statements.identity_note: Spring (p. 35) identifies 'Axininca' as 'Asheninca del Apurucayali', spoken on the Apurucayali river, i.e. exactly ajyi1238; she distinguishes it from Pichis Ashéninka (Payne 1987/J. Payne 1990, where stress is said to refer to the onset) and in ch. 5 uses a second variety 'Axininca 2' only for reduplication, not stress. Stress data are from Payne, Payne & Sánchez 1982 (fn. 17, p. 64).

sources.quote: Payne and Payne demonstrate that stress placement is a low level phonetic phenomenon in Axininca based on a strength scale of syllables, without any reference to grammatical brackets or a cycle. Accordingly, CVN and CVV syllables are generally strong and have some degree of stress, while CV syllables are generally weak and correspondingly unstressed. The normal stress pattern for words with only CV syllables is for every alternate syllable to be stressed beginning with the second syllable. [...] the stress phenomena are predictable based on surface syllable and word shape and a scale of syllable strength versus weakness.

sources.quote: La sílaba fuerte (C)VV(N) siempre está acentuada, mientras que las sílabas débiles /si/ o /čhi/ casi nunca llevan acento. [...] Si una palabra no posee sílabas fuertes, el acento recae en las sílabas alternas, empezando de la segunda sílaba de la palabra. Nótese, sin embargo, que la sílaba CV en posición final de palabra nunca lleva acento [...] La última sílaba fuerte (C)VV(N) o CVN lleva acento primario si se encuentra dentro de las cuatro últimas sílabas de la palabra; de no ser así, el último acento asignado es el primario. (pp. 186, 188, 192)
